shore.text:
The ship that brought you is already being unloaded behind you. Men walk the plank with jars on their shoulders and do not look at the water.

Two of those jars are yours. **Two jars of oil**, a purse you can count without opening, and a name this harbor will write down before it decides what to make of you.

You are standing in **Ugarit**, and Ugarit is a **port** — which in this world means a hinge. North of the coast the **Hittite** king holds the plateau and takes tribute from the cities beneath it. South, **Egypt** is old, rich, and always short of timber and copper. This city lives by standing between the two with a scale and a stylus.

Nobody here speaks your language by accident. The palace keeps its accounts in **Akkadian**, the old trade tongue, pressed into clay with a wedge-shaped stylus. The scribes keep a second script for home: **Ugaritic**, thirty signs, quick to learn and read by almost nobody past the next headland.

You are a **trader**. Courier, translator, and creditor, in whatever order the day asks for. You speak enough **Akkadian** to be understood at a gate, and not enough to be interesting in a palace.

The **market** is up the hill, where grain, oil, and cloth change hands under a scale everyone watches. **Passage** is bought at the harbor, and news lands there before cargo does. The **temple**, the **palace gate**, and the **workshop quarter** each want something different from a stranger.

A porter on the mole looks up at you, holds it a moment too long, and goes back to his basket. You have never been in this harbor.

Nothing here happens quickly — **days pass only when you spend them** — but the light is going, and the gate shuts at dark.

choices.text: Go up the hill to the gate.
Ask the man with the tally board what oil fetches here.

price.text:
"**Oil** is oil," he says, without looking up from the board. "Seven the jar up the hill this week. Nine if the levies are late and the palace decides it is buying."

He wets the stylus, writes something that is not about you, and waits for you to move.

choices.text: Go up the hill to the gate.

sources: Late Bronze Age eastern Mediterranean trade and diplomacy, general
Ugaritic archives and the Hittite vassal treaties, general
provenance.notes: The frame is attested: Ugarit was a Hittite vassal port trading with Egypt and Cyprus, scribes wrote Akkadian and alphabetic Ugaritic, and oil, timber, and copper moved through the harbor. The porter, the tally-man, and every line of dialogue are invented.
